title: Undisputed
full_review:
A heavyweight boxing champion is convicted of rape and sent up the river, where he defends his reputation against the prison's reigning title-holder in the obtuse drama "Undisputed" (Miramax).

Ving Rhames stars as world heavyweight champion George "Iceman" Chambers, a boxer at the peak of his career when it is cut short by a rape conviction. The story echoes that of Mike Tyson's, and it is as dim-witted as some think Tyson is. Director Walter Hill feebly attempts to inject some gravitas into the tedious film, but the result is a wafer-thin plot which broadcasts its narrative turns from miles away. The cardboard characters are so stereotypical as to be laughable. Screenwriters Hill and David Giler must have failed their SATs, since their vocabulary is limited to curses and grunts. Obviously these were inserted as attempts at gritty realism, but the result is a script seriously devoid of any motivating pull to keep the viewer interested.

Sent to the newly built maximum security Sweetwater Prison in the Mojave Desert, Chambers is all attitude and muscle. He considers himself more of a gladiator than an athlete, and refuses to allow anyone to speak to him unless spoken to first. Also serving time at Sweetland is Mendy Ripstein (Peter Falk), whose Mafioso ties can be traced back to Batista's Cuba. A boxing fanatic whose feeble mind is slowing being eaten by senility, Mendy arranges a fight between Chambers and Monroe Hutchen (Wesley Snipes), a rising boxing star who committed a crime that led to a life sentence without the possibility of parole. Hutchen has continued to box in a prison boxing program, arranged by the crooked prison guards and allowed by the yellow-bellied warden, where he has a record of 67 wins and no losses. Mendy, whose connections extend far beyond the prison walls, sees this as the fight of a lifetime and cajoles the reluctant Chambers with promises of time off for good behavior.

The movie mind-numbingly builds toward the climactic encounter between professional boxer and amateur champ, spending no time on character development beyond the necessary essentials. Snipes has very few lines and is mostly seen in solitary confinement working on his toothpick projects. The director shows Snipes meticulously gluing and placing individual toothpicks together which eventually turn into intricate structures such as a Buddhist temple. They are affected scenes which are supposed to convey Hutchen's Zen-like serenity in the face of adversity. But again, Hill's intentions backfire, and Hutchen just cuts a pathetic figure working on an elaborate arts-and-crafts project.

Badly written and executed, "Undisputed" is a poor-man's "Rocky" set inside the clinker. Those who waste their money on the price of admission may be looking for a great escape from this clunker.

Due to menacing scenes of fisticuffs and boxing, fleeting rear nudity and non-stop rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
